transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-24 15:00 PST
Duration: ~54 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Jordan (Redwood SE), Sofia (Redwood CSM), Liam (HP Head of ML), Priya (HP Eng Mgr), Derek (HP Product), Emily (HP Infra)

Summary: quick intake to understand HarborPoint's expected token surges (weekly batch processing + realtime TTR use case), budget ceiling, and whether hosted, dedicated, or private fits. Discussed batching, KV cache behavior, quantization tradeoffs and pilot scope.

Topics: per-token run rate, burst capacity, prefix/KV caching, residency & VPC, pilot sizing, success metrics (latency p95, cost per 1k tokens)

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya: ok thanks everyone for joining, really appreciate it. quick intro? we'll go quick round and then jump into traffic patterns and budgets.
[00:08] Liam: yea hey I'm Liam, head of ML at HarborPoint. we're building a routing assistant and a compliance summarizer, so two fairly different token profiles.
[00:12] Priya: Priya here, I manage infra for ML, curious on deployment options and cost predictability.
[00:16] Derek: Derek, product, mainly here to understand tradeoffs and timeline.
[00:20] Jordan: Jordan Patel, solutions engineer, I'll try to answer the technical perf and pilot questions.
[00:25] Maya: cool, quick context from our side, Red wood (sic) provides hosted API, dedicated GPU pools, and private VPC deployments. we'll focus on economics & pilot sizing today.
[00:33] Emily: a note on security, we need SOC2 + KMS integration for any customer data leaving our VPC; we prefer private but open to options if unit cost lines up.
[00:43] Maya: understood. maybe start with traffic — Liam, what does normal vs surge look like?
[00:46] Liam: baseline is 10 qps for routing assistant mid-day, but we have nightly batch reprocesses that spike token throughput — like 2M tokens over a 1 hour window occasionally, so short sharp bursts. also the summarizer is higher latency tolerant but high token volume.
[01:04] Jordan: got it. so two buckets: low-latency realtime and high-volume batch. good. a couple of levers we typically talk about: batching, KV/prefix cache to avoid re-generation for similar prompts, quantization/8-bit models for cost savings, and routing between hosted/dedicated for burst smoothing.
[01:20] Priya: can you unpack the KV cache stuff? our infra team calls it K V cash sometimes, forgive me.
[01:26] Jordan: yeah, KV cache is basically the attention cache for the decoder — we persist prefix tokens so repeated conversational context doesn't re-tokenize. big gains if you have repeated prefixes or sticky session patterns. in practice we see 20-60% token savings depending on repetition.
[01:42] Liam: 20-60% is attractive. are those savings automatic on hosted or do we need to run a dedicated cluster?
[01:48] Jordan: hosted supports automatic prefix caching and we've got heuristics that keep hot prefixes in memory. Dedicated gives you more control — larger KV eviction windows and you can tune cache sizes, which helps for long sessions. private deployment can do that too but requires config.
[02:02] Maya: and in terms of per-token pricing, we typically quote hosted at X per 1k tokens, dedicated is differ — but importantly you can amortize GPU costs across committed throughput. we'll send numbers after the call.
[02:15] Derek: can you give rough math? like if we do 2M tokens in an hour burst what's the delta hosted vs dedicated?
[02:22] Jordan: rough high-level: with no caching and default model, hosted raw per-token might work out to about $Y per 1k. dedicated with a modest monthly commit often brings unit cost down 30-50% but you have to commit to a baseline. with KV caching and batching you can shave extra 15-40% depending on patterns.
[02:41] Priya: what's the batching latency tradeoff for realtime? we cannot add more than 60ms p99 to our routing flow.
[02:48] Jordan: for routing flows at 10 qps, continuous batching can be kept small — we aim for micro-batching windows of 10-25ms; effectively no visible impact. worst-case p99 impacts come when we queue to fill big batches, but for steady low qps we use small windows.
[03:05] Emily: and if we need burst handling to 2k qps equivalent during batch, do you do automatic burst capacity?
[03:10] Maya: yes hosted supports burst overprovisioning to an extent; dedicated can be configured with burst pools or autoscaling policies. private is more rigid unless you provision extra hardware.
[03:19] Liam: timeline question — we want a pilot in 3 weeks, can you run latency tests and a cost projection fast?
[03:24] Jordan: yes, if you provide sample traces we can run a benchmark that mimics your mix (realtime vs batch) and give per-token projection.
[03:31] Liam: ok we'll try to get traces in next 48 hours.
[03:34] Maya: important note on security — if HarborPoint needs KMS/HSM and audit logs we'll surface our private deployment checklist. hosted has envelope encryption and rotation but some customers with strict compliance pick private.
[03:46] Priya: is there a middle ground? VPC-hosted?
[03:49] Jordan: Redwood Dedicated can be VPC-proxied or a managed VPC with customer peering; it's effectively a bridge — you get isolation with cloud-managed infra.
[03:58] Derek: let's talk numbers — our budget for the initial pilot is $12k/mo — is that workable for a small dedicated slice?
[04:05] Maya: a $12k/mo commit could get you a small dedicated pool, depends on model size and expected sustained tokens. we can map it to throughput: e.g., cpu/gpu hours equivalent and projected tokens per month. we'll share a model.
[04:18] Priya: can you show a 3-scenario model? conservative, expected, optimistic — with cost per 1k tokens and expected p95 latency?
[04:25] Jordan: yes we usually produce three lanes; for conservative assume no KV cache and baseline batch efficiency; expected includes 30% cache savings; optimistic is 50% cache + aggressive quantization.
[04:36] Liam: quantization — we are worried about quality regressions for our summarizer. what do you see in practice?
[04:42] Jordan: 8-bit quantization typically shows minor quality delta on summarization tasks; we recommend doing evals on your prompt set. Redwood Optimize can run automatic regression checks and flag shifts tied to quantized models.
[04:55] Maya: we can include Redwood Optimize for an extra observability layer during pilot so you can measure quality vs cost.
[05:01] Emily: latency SLOs — we need to understand fallback behavior. if a dedicated node is saturated during bursts do you gracefully fall back to hosted or queue?
[05:09] Jordan: we have routing policies: for committed capacity you can set fallback to hosted API (with optional throttling) or to a cheaper model variant. fallbacks can be per-route so critical flows prefer latency-guaranteed fallbacks.
[05:21] Derek: ok that helps. any limitations on data residency or audit logs for hosted fallback?
[05:26] Maya: hosted fallback will be in our standard region unless you choose private/dedicated peering; we log request-level metadata and can provide audit exports for enterprise plans. sensitive payloads you can route to private only.
[05:37] Liam: one more practical: during batch surges our cost spikes unpredictably. can we do token caps or burst limits to keep a monthly ceiling?
[05:45] Jordan: yes you can set per-tenant monthly token caps and per-route throttles; also we support soft-limits with alerts so you'd get notified before hitting the ceiling.
[05:55] Priya: what's typical accuracy of our cost predictions after you run a benchmark with traces? we want +-10% ideally.
[06:01] Jordan: if you give representative traces we typically hit within 10-15% accuracy; worst cases are when user behavior shifts abruptly, but we include sensitivity lanes.
[06:12] Maya: quick recap so we're aligned: HarborPoint will share 7 days of traces + top prompts; Redwood will run a bench and return a 3-scenario unit econ model, and a recommended pilot config (hosted vs small dedicated). we'll include security docs and pilot pricing.
[06:25] Liam: sounds good.
[06:27] Derek: one last question — competitors came up, we also evaluated Vertex AI and an internal on-prem solution. what's your differentiation on predictable unit cost?
[06:36] Maya: the differentiation is the engine + ops: we provide transparent per-token breakdown, caching/batching knobs exposed in Console, and dedicated pools with SLA-backed latency targets so you can predict costs and performance.
[06:47] Priya: ok we have enough for now, thanks.
[06:50] Maya: thanks everyone. we'll follow up with the spreadsheet and security packet. next call: bench review week of 2026-02-02.

End of transcript.
